lead: A 300 mm model in a laboratory and a 3 m runner at a hill site cannot be compared by their speeds or discharges, because head and size are mixed into every reading. Unit quantities divide the head out: unit speed, unit discharge and unit power say what the same machine would do under exactly one metre of head. Specific speed divides out size too, leaving one number that fixes the type of turbine. Manufacturers, tender documents and electricity utilities use it before any machine is drawn.
prereq: You need: the Pelton wheel in 6.4, the Francis and Kaplan runners in 6.5, and the similarity laws and model studies of Unit 5, Boundary Layer and Dimensional Analysis.

sections.h3: Unit quantities: dividing out the head

blocks.text: A turbine is a shape, not a size. Two runners are geometrically similar when every length of one is the same multiple of the matching length of the other: same vane angles, same number of buckets, same proportions. Inside one such family every velocity in the machine is proportional to √(2gH), with g = 9.81 m/s² and H the net head in metres.

The runner speed u, the jet speed and the flow speed all rise as √H. Discharge is area × velocity, and area goes as D², where D is the runner diameter in metres. Three measured quantities therefore range roughly as N ∝ √H/D, Q ∝ D²√H and P ∝ D²H^{3/2}, with P the shaft power.
N₁ = N/√H      Q₁ = Q/√H      P₁ = P/H^{3/2}
blocks.where: N is the actual speed in rpm, N₁ the unit speed in rpm; Q is the actual discharge in m³/s, Q₁ the unit discharge in m³/s; P is the shaft power in kW, P₁ the unit power in kW; H is the net head in metres.

blocks.text: Read them as a what-if. N₁ is the speed this machine would run at under exactly 1 m of head, Q₁ the discharge it would then pass, P₁ the power it would then give. They also tell you how one machine behaves at a new head: raise the head from H to 4H and the speed doubles, the discharge doubles, and the power becomes 4^{1.5} = 8 times.
They do not remove size. A 2 m runner and its half-scale model have different unit quantities even when the shapes match, because N₁ ∝ 1/D, Q₁ ∝ D² and P₁ ∝ D². Only the head has been divided out.

sections.h3: Specific speed: one number for the type

blocks.text: Size is still inside the unit quantities. Divide it out and one number remains, the specific speed. Start from the similarity rules: Q ∝ D²√H and P ∝ QH ∝ D²H^{3/2}, so D ∝ √P / H^{3/4}. Speed goes as N ∝ √H/D, which gives N ∝ H^{5/4}/√P. Rearranged, N√P/H^{5/4} is the same for every machine of the family, whatever its size.

blocks.where: N_s is the specific speed, quoted in rpm, but it is not a running speed; only the form ω√Q/(gH)^{3/4} is fully dimensionless. N is the actual running speed in rpm; P is the shaft power in kW; H is the net head in metres.

blocks.text: Some books define specific speed from discharge instead. Then N_s = N√Q / H^{3/4}, with Q in m³/s and H in metres. The two definitions give different numbers for the same machine and are not interchangeable, so always state which one you used. The discharge form is the usual one for pumps, see Unit 7, Centrifugal and Reciprocating Pumps.
Dividing the units out as well gives a dimensionless shape number, ω√Q/(gH)^{3/4}, with ω the angular speed in rad/s. It carries the same information with no units attached.

The number is a shape label. A high N_s means a short, fat runner that passes a large discharge at low head; a low N_s means a tall, narrow runner working on a small discharge at high head. That is why the type follows from N_s alone, before any drawing is made.

sections.h3: Scaling a machine with these numbers

blocks.text: A tender fixes the head the site gives and the power the grid needs. The specific speed then fixes the speed and the shape family, and the unit quantities fix the size.

items: Note the head H and the power P the site can supply.
Read a trial N_s from the band table for that head; the type of turbine follows.
Find the speed from N = N_s H^{5/4} / √P, then round it to a synchronous value such as 3000/n rpm for a 50 Hz supply (3000, 1500, 1000, 750 ...).
Fix the runner size from a similar model: N₁ ∝ 1/D and Q₁ ∝ D², so D grows as the square root of the discharge per metre of head.

blocks.text: In the worked example, 5000 kW at 300 rpm under 80 m gives N_s = 88.66, inside the Francis band, with unit speed 33.54 rpm, unit discharge 0.805 m³/s and unit power 6.988 kW. Scale-up is not free: a model and its prototype share N_s only while they stay truly similar, and efficiency rises with size, so the predicted prototype power is corrected upward. Comparison of running points is in 6.8.

figure.caption: One number sorts the three turbines: Pelton up to 60, Francis 60 to 300, Kaplan above 300. The worked example's 88.66 sits inside the middle band.

spec.aria: A left-to-right chain rising in specific speed: Pelton at 10 to 60, then Francis at 60 to 300, then Kaplan at 300 and above.

examples.question: A turbine develops 5000 kW at 300 rpm under a net head of 80 m, with a discharge of 7.2 m³/s. Find the specific speed (power form), the unit speed, the unit discharge and the unit power, and name the type of turbine.
steps: List the data with units: P = 5000 kW, N = 300 rpm, H = 80 m, Q = 7.2 m³/s.
88.66 lies between 60 and 300, so the machine is a Francis turbine.
examples.answer: Specific speed N_s = 88.66 rpm, which is a Francis turbine; unit speed 33.54 rpm, unit discharge 0.805 m³/s and unit power 6.988 kW.
examples.check:
import math
P = 5000.0
N = 300.0
H = 80.0
Q = 7.2
ns = N * math.sqrt(P) / H**1.25
n1 = N / math.sqrt(H)
q1 = Q / math.sqrt(H)
p1 = P / H**1.5
print(round(ns, 2))
print(round(n1, 2))
print(round(q1, 3))
print(round(p1, 3))

traps: Using the power form N_s = N√P/H^{5/4} and the discharge form N_s = N√Q/H^{3/4} in the same answer. They give different numbers; state the definition you used before substituting.
Feeding P in watts or H in centimetres into a formula built for kW and metres. 5000 kW is not 5000; it is 5 000 000 W, and the answer changes by a factor of about 31.6.

Writing H^{3/2} where H^{5/4} belongs, or squaring H in the specific speed. The 5/4 exponent cannot be found by cancelling units, because N_s in this metric form is not dimensionless. Get it by combining N ∝ √H/D with P ∝ D²H^{3/2}, or simply remember it. Only ω√Q/(gH)^{3/4} is dimensionless.
Forgetting the square root: N√P means N times √P. With P = 5000 kW, √P = 70.71, so the numerator is 300 × 70.71 = 21213. Writing √(N P) would wrongly give √1500000 = 1224.7.
Calling N_s a running speed. A turbine with N_s = 88.66 rpm usually runs at 300 rpm or more; the unit rpm appear in the formula only as bookkeeping.

quiz.q: Define specific speed of a turbine from power, and give its units.
quiz.a: N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}, with N in rpm, P the shaft power in kW and H the net head in metres. It is quoted in rpm, though it is a shape number, not a real speed.

quiz.q: Write the unit power formula and state the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: P₁ = P/H^{3/2}, with P in kW, H in metres and P₁ in kW.

quiz.q: Specific speed is the same for a model and its geometrically similar prototype, but unit speed is not. Why?
quiz.a: Specific speed divides out both head and size, so only the shape survives. Unit speed still contains the diameter, because N₁ ∝ 1/D: a half-scale runner turns twice as fast per metre of head.

quiz.q: A turbine runs at 150 rpm under a net head of 25 m and delivers 800 kW. Find its specific speed on the power definition and name the type.
The turbine of the previous question is run at the same setting but with the head raised from 25 m to 36 m. Find the new speed and new power.
Unit A runs at 500 rpm, 100 kW, 200 m head. Unit B runs at 200 rpm, 2000 kW, 15 m head. Compute both specific speeds and say which is the reaction machine with a draft tube.
Two turbines of identical shape and head run at different speeds. Which quantity is unchanged, and what does that tell you about using specific speed to compare them?
quiz.a: Both are geometrically similar, so their specific speeds are equal; only the sizes and speeds differ. The constant N_s is exactly the point: it labels the shape family and the type of turbine, and size or speed changes leave it alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Model acceptance tests for large hydro units follow IEC 60193, which uses the dimensionless specific speed and efficiency scale-up rules of this kind. Modern design uses CFD to shape a runner once N_s is fixed, because N_s settles the meridional proportions before any blade is drawn. Pumps borrow the same number, and the suction specific speed predicts cavitation limits on the inlet side.
